title: Microorganisms
standard_text: Microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses) are too small to see without a microscope; some are useful (in food, decay and medicine) and some cause disease; good hygiene prevents the spread of disease. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 5, Quarter 2: Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 2: Living Things): useful micro-organisms, micro-organisms and decay, pathogens and disease, spread of disease and defense against disease. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Most micro-organisms are harmless or useful.
key_sub: Hygiene and vaccines stop diseases spreading.
body_html:
How to think about it

Micro-organisms are living things too small to see without a microscope: bacteria, protists, some fungi (yeast) and viruses (which can only reproduce inside cells).

Some cause disease: tuberculosis (bacteria), HIV and flu (viruses), malaria (a protist) and thrush (a fungus). Many are useful: yeast in bread, bacteria in yoghurt and amasi, and decomposers in compost. Washing hands, clean water, vaccines and antibiotics (for bacteria) help to prevent and treat disease.

Example

Which micro-organism makes bread rise?

A fungus

Answer: yeast

Example

Can antibiotics cure flu?

Flu is caused by a virus.

Answer: no

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all micro-organisms are harmful.
  • Thinking antibiotics kill viruses.
  • Thinking viruses are cells.

items.q: Which cells make antibodies?
items.e: Phagocytes engulf pathogens.

items.q: Can cholera be treated with antibiotics?
c: only if a vaccine is also given
items.e: Cholera is caused by a bacterium. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.

items.q: Can influenza be treated with antibiotics?
c: only if a vaccine is also given
items.e: Influenza is caused by a virus. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.

items.q: What is an antigen?
c: a molecule on the surface of a pathogen that triggers the making of antibodies
a type of white blood cell
items.e: Each pathogen has its own antigens.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes the common cold?
items.e: Antibiotics can treat bacterial diseases, but not viral ones.

items.q: Why must a new influenza vaccine be made each year?
c: The old vaccine stops working in the refrigerator.
The virus mutates, so its antigens change.
items.e: Memory cells may not recognize the new antigens.

items.q: How do antibiotic-resistant bacteria arise?
c: The patient becomes resistant to the antibiotic.
A random mutation makes some bacteria resistant; they survive the antibiotic and multiply.
items.e: This is natural selection.

items.q: Why should a patient finish the whole course of antibiotics?
c: to kill all the bacteria, so resistant ones are less likely to survive and multiply
items.e: Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes pneumococcal disease?
items.e: Antibiotics can treat bacterial diseases, but not viral ones.

items.q: What causes pneumococcal disease?
items.e: Influenza is viral; pneumococcal disease is bacterial.

fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches and tiredness

items.q: What type of pathogen causes COVID-19?

items.q: What is herd immunity?
c: When most people are vaccinated, the disease cannot spread easily, protecting those who are not immune.
items.e: This protects babies and people who cannot be vaccinated.

items.q: How is influenza mainly spread?

items.q: Why does a vaccinated person not become ill when infected?
c: Memory cells make antibodies quickly, before the pathogen can multiply.
The vaccine stays in the blood for ever as antibodies.
The vaccine kills all pathogens in the air.
items.e: The secondary response is faster and larger.

items.q: A fetus receives antibodies across the placenta. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: How does the skin help defend the body?
c: It acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions.
They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
items.e: First and second lines of defense.

items.q: A person bitten by a snake is given an injection of ready-made antibodies (antivenom). Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Which part of the body's defenses does this: “Engulf and digest pathogens”?
c: cilia in the trachea and bronchi
items.e: First and second lines of defense.

items.q: A traveler is given a hepatitis A vaccine before a trip. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Which part of the body's defenses does this: “Acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions”?
c: hairs and mucus in the nose
items.e: First and second lines of defense.

items.q: How do bacteria make us ill?
c: They reproduce quickly and may make toxins that damage tissues.
items.e: Toxins.

items.q: A patient with a dangerous infection is given a serum of antibodies from a donor. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: How do viruses make us ill?
c: They live and reproduce inside cells, damaging them.
They make toxins outside cells only.
items.e: Cell damage.

items.q: How do antitoxins help defend the body?
c: They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
They neutralize toxins made by bacteria.
It acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions.
items.e: First and second lines of defense.

items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Which is a way to reduce the spread of disease?
